messages.subject: including coordinates as fixed effects in a spatial model?
messages.subject_clean: including coordinates as fixed effects in a spatial model?
messages.body_plain: I had a question about including the x or y component of a coordinate as a fixed effect in an INLA model that already includes a spatial random effect. Is that somewhat redundant to include in a model like this? I guess I've seen a few analyses now where latitude or longitude (or both) were also used as fixed effects, and I was considering using latitude in my own analysis to understand how laying date varies with latitude and temperature anomaly at that particular location (whether it was a warm or cold spring for example). Is that latitude effect already captured when I include the spatial field in the model?

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] including coordinates as fixed effects in a spatial model?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] including coordinates as fixed effects in a spatial model?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jason,

this depends a bit on the situation; both options can be sensible.
With x&y as explicit covariates, the spatial random field component
can focus on non-linear effects, with a shorter correlation range,
than if x&y are left out, and the field has to capture both large
scale spatial linear trends, needing a long correlation range, as well
as smaller features.  But if there are large scale non-linear features
that are so large that they can't really be distinguished from the
linear trends, then having both x&y and the field may make the
coefficients non-identifiable.  This is normally not an issue in
prediction/smoothing settings, but requires extra care if the
parameters themselves are of interest.  Sometimes one can try to
impose trend-equal-zero constraints on the spatial field component,
but that isn't always ideal.

Personally, if I suspect there to be possible latitude and/or
east/west effects, I would include x&y as explicit covariates, and
then treat the combined effect of x&y&field as a single component, and
not try to tease apart the individual contributions.

Finn

messages.subject: Error in inla.create.sn.cache() : inla.require("sn") is not TRUE
messages.subject_clean: Error in inla.create.sn.cache() : inla.require("sn") is not TRUE
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I am trying to run one of the practicals for inlabru using the following:
data(gorillas, package = "inlabru")
nests <- gorillas$nests
mesh <- gorillas$mesh
boundary <- gorillas$boundary
matern <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh,
                              prior.sigma = c(0.1, 0.01),
                              prior.range = c(5, 0.01))
cmp <- coordinates ~ mySmooth(map = coordinates,
                              model = matern) +
                          Intercept

fit <- lgcp(cmp, nests, samplers = boundary)

lambda <- predict(fit, pixels(mesh), ~ exp(mySmooth + Intercept))

The predict function fails with the following error:
Error in inla.create.sn.cache() : inla.require("sn") is not TRUE

I can't seem to find a help file for that error or any reference to either function and so don't know what might be going wrong. Any insight as to what's going on here would be most appreciated. Session info below if it's helpful.

messages.body_plain:
It appears that a number of the dependencies (e.g., 'graph' and 'RgraphViz') have been removed from cran (including old versions)? There are also some references <https://community.rstudio.com/t/cant-install-psych-dependencies-mnormt/68770> to a problem with gfortran when installing mnormt. I've had to do some fiddling with my compilers to make Stan run on Catalina, so this may be part of the issue. I'm going to see if updating fixes things, but leave this here in case someone else runs into this. Will report back after the update.

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

from what I recall, the reason I never wrote a complete
inla.segment-to-sp converter is the handling of holes; the
inla.segment objects doesn't explicitly label edges as holes or not;
it only keeps track of what is on the inside and outside of each edge
segment. To identify holes, it would need to build a mesh, which
_does_ correctly identify the emergent holes from the segment
representation. It's not in principle difficult, I just never got
around to it.

Similarly, sf did not yet exist when the sp support was added to INLA,
and there hasn't been time to add sf support since when sf appeared;
it would touch on so much of the mesh related code that it would be
better to add that support properly as part of converting the fmesher
interface to a separate package, which is on my TODO-list!

Finn

messages.body_plain:
I have been getting lots of warnings working with the new version of sf and then converting to sp Spatial objects to work with INLA. It is great to hear you are working on updating to the new CRS methods. I hope this can resolve this for me. Also very excited to see INLA moving to github!

Anyway, just for your information as you move towards updating to R 4 and new CRS methods, I thought I'd post my problem, in case it helps:

When using inla.mesh.2d with crs = INLA::inla.CRS("sphere"), and using sp data that was in "EPSG:4326" projection converted from sf, I get more than 50 warnings of this variety:

1: In showSRID(SRS_string, format = "PROJ", multiline = "NO") :
  Discarded ellps unknown in CRS definition: +proj=geocent +R=1 +units=m +no_defs
2: In showSRID(SRS_string, format = "PROJ", multiline = "NO") :
  Discarded datum unknown in CRS definition
3: In showSRID(SRS_string, format = "PROJ", multiline = "NO") :
  Discarded ellps unknown in CRS definition: +proj=geocent +R=1 +units=m +no_defs
4: In showSRID(SRS_string, format = "PROJ", multiline = "NO") :
  Discarded datum unknown in CRS definition

When I plot the mesh in rgl, it looks okay, however, if I use the mesh in INLA::inla.mesh.project, with some coordinates also converted to sp from sf with "EPSG:4326" projection I get the same kind of warnings, and then when I plot the points on the globe, they don't look quite right especially near the poles.

I'm stuck at this point! I don't know whether to trust the results, given the warnings, and the plot not looking right. This code used to work before I upgraded my sf version (and presumably with it my PROJ6 version). But I guess I will wait for that blog post you mentioned which will hopefully shed light on this!

Thanks for all your work on INLA!

Cheers,

Russell

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
The blog post has been held up by teaching and other work, but the short answer is that the current version of inla does have proj6 support. If the function INLA::inla.has_PROj6() exists and returns TRUE you have a new INLA and proj6.
Even with the new version you will still receive lots of warnings (but different warnings than before) that come from the rgdal package, but most of these can be ignored, since they only relate to the backwards compatibility behaviour of rgdal for the old proj4 strings, that are now mostly ignored, and the actual projection info stored as a “WKT” string. The new inLa version has some tools to help work with those, but the bulk of the warnings can be turned off in rgdal. (And as I understand it they will deactivate these compatibility warnings by default in a future version)

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

 I need to use the excursions.inla function, but the available documentation is scarce.

This is my model formula for estimating PM10 daily concentrations in Italy, for the month of January.

as.formula(lpm10~Intercept+dust+aod550.s+log.pbl00.s+log.pbl12.s+sp.s+t2m.s+tp.s+ptp.s+q_dem.s+i_surface.s+d_a1.s-1)->myformula

#spde with autoregressive AR(1) structure:

update(myformula,.~.+f(id_centralina,model="iid")+f(i,model=spde,group = i.group,control.group = list(model="ar1",hyper=list(theta=theta_hyper))))->myformula

  #spde definition
   inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh=mesh,alpha=2,constr=FALSE,prior.range = c(150,0.8),prior.sigma = c(0.8,0.2))->spde

  #n_giorni: the number of days in January, 1..31
  inla.spde.make.index(name="i",n.spde=spde$n.spde,n.group = n_giorni)->iset

  inla(myformula,
         data=inla.stack.data(mystack,spde=spde),
         family ="gaussian",
         verbose=TRUE,
         control.compute = list(openmp.strategy="pardiso.parallel",cpo=TRUE,waic=TRUE,dic=TRUE,config=TRUE),
         control.fixed = list(prec.intercept = 0.001, prec=1,mean.intercept=0),
         control.predictor =list(A=inla.stack.A(mystack),compute=TRUE) )->>inla.out

Now, I have my inla.out object. How can I use excursions.inla to calculate the excursion function for one specific day in January (e.g, 29 January)?  The excursions.inla interface has the argument "ind" to set "indices"? Is that argument that I have to use? If yes, how?

If I try something like this below, I get an error:

excurions.inla(inla.out,tag="training",stack=mystack,type=">",u=log(50),method="QC",ind=which(iset$i.group==29))

What's wrong? How to calculate excursions sets for one specific day?

Thanks in advance
Guido

Hi Sol,

If you are using inlabru, then plotting predictions of fixed effects is pretty straight forward. See instructions from Thierry Onkelinx here: https://www.muscardinus.be/2018/07/inlabru-bru/.

Best,
Tim

On Thursday, June 25, 2020 at 2:49:11 AM UTC-6, S Milne wrote:
> Hi all,
>
> I'm following up on a previous topic about plotting covariate effects from inla (in this case inlabru).
> I'm trying to plot the marginals.fixed from my model, with the 0.05 & 0.975 CI on either side and mean in the middle, as shown here.
> https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/113940/in-r-and-inla-how-do-i-graph-results-of-rw2-model
>
> I think my hang up is that I I think the 'ID' object here refers to the locations of the predictions, and I don't know what the equivalent of that would be in my model.
>
> I have 8 fixed effects in my model, and if I could present them this way it be really handy in terms of explaining how the predicted density of my predictions relates to values from these continuous spatial covariates.
>
> ###

>

> Sol

messages.body_plain: I've got a couple of NVIDIA Jetson development kits and want to get r-inla running on them. They run Ubuntu 18.04 LTS on multi-core arm64 modules. Is there a Linux binary for this architecture? If not, where's the source code - I can probably build them from source.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Linux binaries for arm64 / building from source?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Linux binaries for arm64 / building from source?
messages.body_plain:
I put at

	hrue.r-inla-download.org/build64.tgz <http://hrue.r-inla-download.org/build64.tgz>

the build directory I use for Ubuntu18.04 on x86.

I do

	export INLA_TAG=Version_20.07.16-1
	make update

and it will download that 'tag' from the git-repo, and compile the
binaries.

you have to use the TAG that is the same as your INLA version

> inla.version("version")
[1] "20.07.16-1"

and then I find the binaries at

	local/bin/inla
	local/bin/inla.mkl
	local/bin/fmesher

you can set

	library(INLA)
	inla.setOption(inla.call='/home/.../bin/inla')
	inla.setOption(fmesher.call='/home/.../bin/fmesher')

to use that binary

you need to recompile the libs for arm64, like

	make -C gmrflib clean
	make -C inlaprog clean
	make taucs
	make amd

etc

hope it works!
H

messages.body_plain:
Hello,
Can you clarify the appropriate syntax for continuous covariates? Your response seems to suggest that the following is correct:
model <- coordinates ~ continuous.cov(map = continuous.cov.spdf, model="linear")

however, the tutorial on inlabru.org <http://inlabru.org> suggests this is necessary:
f.elev <- function(x,y) {
  # turn coordinates into SpatialPoints object:
  spp <- SpatialPoints(data.frame(x=x,y=y))
  # attach the appropriate coordinate reference system (CRS)
  proj4string(spp) <- CRS(proj4string(elev))
  # Extract elevation values at spp coords, from our elev SpatialGridDataFrame
  v <- over(spp, elev)
  v[is.na(v)] <- 0 # NAs are a problem! Remove them
  return(v$elevation)
}
emdl <- coordinates ~ beta.elev(map = f.elev(x,y), model = "linear")

However, when I try the latter with a different covariate (named `roughness`), I get the error mentioned above:

Error in match.names(clabs, names(xi)) :
  names do not match previous names

Has the syntax changed since the tutorial was written? Or can you point me to which 'names' are mismatching when this error is thrown?
Thank you,
M

messages.subject: inlabru::lgcp with environmental covariate and iid observer effect
messages.subject_clean: inlabru::lgcp with environmental covariate and iid observer effect
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am trying to build a species distribution model using inlabru::lgcp. I have some conceptual and technical questions.

Conceptual question. Take the gorillas dataset. Imagine there were 5 different observers collecting the data and all very different in terms of skill. Say you wanted to add an iid observer effect. How would this work? Does lgcp generate quadrature points under the hood based on the samplers argument? What would be the level(s) of the observer random effect for the quadrature points? Maybe lgcp doesn't use quadrature points, so this is a pointless question.

Technical questions. How would one add an iid observer effect to the gorillas example? I have tried adding one to the gnests dataframe and model statement (below), and it runs. Did I do it right? I also tried adding a fixed effect to the gnests dataframe and model statement (below), and it runs. Did I do it right?  I looked over David Borchers slides for adding a fixed covariate to an lgcp model by extracting it from a spatial pixels dataframe, but it breaks. Any ideas here?

Thanks for any help!

Tim

Here is some code.

# libraries
library(inlabru); library(INLA)

# get data
data(gorillas)
gnests <- gorillas$nests
mesh <- gorillas$mesh
boundary <- gorillas$boundary
gcounts <- gorillas$plotsample$counts
gcov <- gorillas$gcov
pxl <- pixels(mesh, mask=boundary, nx = 500, ny = 400)

# plot data
ggplot() + gg(boundary) +
  gg(gnests) +
  coord_fixed() + xlab("x") + ylab("y")

##### fit model with intercept and spatial field
mdl1 <- coordinates ~ spat(map=coordinates,
                           model=inla.spde2.matern(mesh, constr=F)) +
                      Intercept
init.tutorial()
fit1 <- lgcp(components=mdl1, data=gnests, samplers=boundary)
summary(fit1)

# what does this output message mean?
"Warning message: In if (eff$model == 'spde2') { :
  the condition has length > 1 and only the first element will be used"

# plot density from intercept and spatial field
lgcp.dens1 <- predict(fit1, pxl, ~ exp(spat+Intercept))
ggplot() + gg(lgcp.dens1) + gg(boundary, alpha = 0) +
  gg(gnests) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette="Spectral")

##### make hypothetical observer iid random and season fixed effects
gnests@data$group_int <- as.numeric(factor(gnests@data$group))
n_groups <- max(gnests@data$group_int)
gnests@data$season_eff <- as.numeric(factor(gnests@data$group))-1.5
summary(gnests)

# plot hypothetical effects, note that there seems to be little correlation
# with density, so you might not expect these to be important
ggplot() + gg(boundary) +
  gg(data=gnests, aes(color=group_int)) +
  coord_fixed() + xlab("x") + ylab("y")
ggplot() + gg(boundary) +
  gg(data=gnests, aes(color=season_eff)) +
  coord_fixed() + xlab("x") + ylab("y")

##### fit model with added hypothetical iid random observer effect
mdl2 <- coordinates ~ spat(map=coordinates,
                           model=inla.spde2.matern(mesh, constr=F)) +
  grp(map=group_int, model="iid", n=n_groups) +
  Intercept
fit2 <- lgcp(components=mdl2, data=gnests, samplers=boundary)
summary(fit2)

# plot density from intercept and spatial field
lgcp.dens2 <- predict(fit2, pxl, ~ exp(spat+Intercept))
ggplot() + gg(lgcp.dens2) + gg(boundary, alpha = 0) +
  gg(gnests) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette="Spectral")

##### fit model with added hypothetical iid observer random and season fixed effects
mdl3 <- coordinates ~ spat(map=coordinates,
                           model=inla.spde2.matern(mesh, constr=F)) +
  grp(map=group_int, model="iid", n=n_groups) +
  seas(map=season_eff, model="linear") + Intercept
fit3 <- lgcp(components=mdl3, data=gnests, samplers=boundary)
summary(fit3)

# plot density from intercept and spatial field
lgcp.dens3 <- predict(fit3, pxl, ~ exp(spat+Intercept))
ggplot() + gg(lgcp.dens3) + gg(boundary, alpha = 0) +
  gg(gnests) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette="Spectral")

##### fit model with vegetation fixed effect as shown by David Borchers. in
# this case, values of the fixed effect are extracted from a spatial pixels
# dataframe for gnest locations. but things are broken. any advice on how to
# fix it? any advice on how to add random intercept for a hypothetical group
# variable, such as observer ID?
mdl4 <- coordinates ~ veg(map=gcov$vegetation, model="factor") - Intercept
fit4 <- lgcp(components=mdl4, data=gnests, samplers=boundary,
             domain=list(coordinates=mesh),
             options=list(control.fixed=list(expand.factor.strategy="inla")))

Hi,

I'd need to see the exact code that gives the error, and the
traceback() output to have any chance of debugging that, since it
doesn't seem to be at all the same as the previous problem in the
thread (the spurious f() calls), and there are no calls to
match.names() in the inlabru code.

But yes, the tutorial was initially written for an earlier version
where the direct use of a SpatialPixelsDataFrame object instead of an
"f.extract.covariate()" function call hadn't been implemented. If I
recall correctly, the second half of the tutorial does use that new
functionality, but gives an incorrect reason for why. The
f.evel()-like code is now part of the package, and the user only needs
to make their own if the built-in version can't do the right thing,
for whatever reason.

Do make sure to check this on the github devel branch version, since
there are some bug fixes there that are not on CRAN. Soon there will
also be an entirely new version that should clear up most of these
issues.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

the warning message for summary() is a known bug. Please ignore the
inlabru summary function until the next major release, and use
  INLA:::summary.inla(fit)
instead.

For lgcp models, the difficulty is that it's not (just) the observed
points that are the data, but also all information where there _could
have been_ points.
So for different observers, we need to know where/when each observer
tried to find nests. E.g. did they each survey the entire region
independently, or were they responsible for their own part of space?

In the former case, it's no longer a simple lgcp observation model,
since the nests are fixed, leading to dependence between the
observers. Building 5 separate estimates, one for each observer, is an
option, but it's not clear how to combine those estimates while
retaining correct uncertainty information. The correct solution would
involve implementing the full multivariate detection process
likelihood (possible but we haven't done it).

In the latter case, where each observer is responsible for their own
disjoint part of space, then a spatial grid covariate linked to an iid
model would be ok. I distrust even my own code dealing with factors in
R, so better to construct a simple integer valued covariate with
values 1,2, ..., 5, as a SpatialPixelsDataFrame (or
SpatialGridDataFrame) and use "iid". However, identifiability becomes
an issue, so a more trusted "factor" model implementation in inlabru
would be preferable. I'm looking at that as part of the next major
update (running a few months behind the plans due to the pandemic).

For the problem you have with the vegetation covariate, please make
sure you use the github devel version for testing (the devel branch
doesn't yet contain the major updates, but does contain some other bug
fixes), and provide the full error&warning messages and traceback()
output to help me debug.

Finn

Thanks,

Aashna

messages.subject: Best practices for evaluating different specifications of the spatial component in lgcp?
messages.subject_clean: Best practices for evaluating different specifications of the spatial component in lgcp?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I am working on some presence-only species distribution models and am getting some substantially different predictions of lambda based on the spatial smoothing component (e.g., using different max.edge lengths, altering the priors for for the inla.spde2.pcmatern specification, etc). My concern is that the spatial component is overfitting the data (evidenced by sharp drops in lambda just beyond the edge of the presence locations; see the attached image). I've tried using model selection based on a saturated model containing all of my covariates and different formulations of the spatial effect, but the "overfit" (i.e., the one with the tightly constrained spatial term model consistently outperforms models with 'smoother' spatial terms. This suggests to me that using the saturated model is, perhaps, not the best way to select the 'appropriate' formulation of inla.spde2.pcmatern. I've tried using the meshbuilder() mesh assessment tools (that's how I ended up using the 'overfit' specification for the mesh), but that seems to focus on the theoretical properties of the mesh (not the estimation of the random field based on the mesh AND priors).I'm wondering whether others have a reference or "best practice" for choosing among competing formulations of the spatial component? Any suggestions would be greatly appreciated.
Best,
Matt Williamson

messages.subject_clean: Can I conduct spatial modeling when one covariate is categorical?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I want to model distribution of geochemical element concentration using INLA-SPDE.  One of the covariate for modeling fixed effect is categorical.

I followed the strategy as in classical regression, i.e. converting the categorical covariate into several dummy variables, and kept part of them for modeling.

The following is a screenshot of the preprocessed data, the dummy varaibles being indicated by columns of "Lithos" and "Intrus" (part of the complete data file named "geochem.csv" with 623 lines):

The following is my code:

library(INLA)
## -----------prepare data --------------
rawdata<-read.table('geochem.csv', sep=",", header=TRUE, encoding="UTF-8")
coo<-rawdata[, c("X", "Y")]
coo<-as.matrix(coo)
x1 <- rawdata[, "Faults"]
x2 <- rawdata[, "Lithos"]
x3 <- rawdata[, "Intrus"]
y<-rawdata[, "RPC2"]

## ------ Modeling with INLA ------------
# 1. Mesh
mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(
  coo,
  max.edge=c(0.1, 0.2),
  cutoff=0.005)
plot(mesh, asp=1); points(coo, col='red', cex=0.5)

# 2. Define the projector matrix
A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh=mesh, loc=coo)

# 3. Build the SPDE model on the mesh
spde <- inla.spde2.matern(
  mesh=mesh, alpha=1.5)

# 4. Create a stack data
stk.e <- inla.stack(tag='est',
                    data=list(y=y),
                    A=list(A, 1),
                    effects=list(
                      s=1:spde$n.spde,
                      data.frame(b0=1, x1=x1, x2=x2, x3=x3)))

# 5. Fit
formula <- y ~ 0 + b0 + x1 + x2 + x3
  f(s, model=spde) ## RF term
res <- inla(formula, data=inla.stack.data(stk.e),
            control.predictor=list(A = inla.stack.A(stk.e)))# projector

res$summary.fixed

Now my questions are:
(1) whether my code is right for dealing with the dummy variables, especially the lines of defining "inla.stack";
(2) whether do I need to normalize the continuous covariate "Faults" into the range of [0, 1] before inla modeling?
(3) the coordinates x, y have been translated and scaled into [0, 1], so whether the parameters "max.edge" and "cutoff" are correctly set when building the mesh?

Is there anyone that could give me a help? Thank you.

Best regards,
Kuan

messages.body_plain:
Thanks, Finn. I found a nice paper that demonstrates building a IPPM with presence-only data using the weighted logistic regression trick of Fithian and Hastie. They use the strategy I mentioned above, creating 10 quadrature points for each individual in the dataset and adding an "iid" to the logistic regression model. I will now experiment with adding a spatial SPDE effect to the weighted regression model and see what I get. Seems like this would yield something similar to the lgcp model, but that is from the perspective of an ecologist, hacking his way toward an acceptable solution!

Paper: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/1365-2656.13087

messages.subject_clean: Can I conduct spatial modeling when one covariate is categorical?
messages.body_plain:
This looks fine to me. You could compare your code with this tutorial that shows how to build a similar model with inla versus inlabru: https://www.muscardinus.be/2018/07/inlabru-bru/

Q1: the stack statement looks OK to me, but I am not sure about the A=list(A, 1) and b0=1 at the same time. Hopefully someone else can check that -- this part always confuses me.

Q2: you don't have to center or scale the continuous covariate if you don't want. but there are advantages to doing it related to computing stability and setting/understanding priors and interpreting coefficients. E.g., Andrew Gelman has a paper on scaling continuous and categorical variables so that beta coefficients are comparable.

Q3: if the mesh and data are all on a consistently scaled coordinate system, you should be fine. the only exception is if some functions that you use downstream in your analysis are looking for a consistent CRS. you might get errors that crs's don't match.

messages.body_plain:
Good answers from Tim!

I’ll add that the b0=1 part is fine, since the data.frame will expand it to an all-1 column matching the lengths of the other columns.

>From the visible values of the continuous covariate, I would recommend not scaling it, since it’s already on a decent scale. In any case, scaling based on empirical variance etc should be avoided, since it’s so fragile with respect to data subsampling and other data set changes, such as for spatial prediction. When/if scaling is needed for numerical reasons, I would instead recommend choosing the scaling by hand (e.g. as a whole power of 10).

Finn

messages.body_plain:
The likely issue with having only a sparse numerical integration scheme within each observer comes when including a flexible spatial effect. With just global covariates a small number of integration points is fine, but for mesh based SPDEs there’s a pivoting effect that kicks in within the triangles, and the approximation isn’t robust unless the integration points “tie down” the function near observed presences. This is why we use integration points at all the mesh nodes for lgcp likelihoods; more sparse schemes don’t work.  Perhaps placing pseudo absences also at all the presences (in some way that avoids bias...) _might_ be a way around the problem in your case.

Our work in progress approach to these models can avoid that problem more generally.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am analyzing population abundance using a hurdle model.

The probability sub-model follows a Bernoulli distribution:
logit(p) = intercept_z+ f(year_z, model=“iid”)

The positive sub-model follows a zero-truncated Poisson distribution:
log(lambda) = intercept_y + f(year_y, model=“iid”)

I would like to combine year effects in the two sub-models and get year effect on population abundance.

Here is my equation:
1 / ( 1 + exp(-f(year_z)))*exp(f(year_y))

Is it correct?

Thanks,
Ruby

messages.subject_clean: The sparse parametrisation of the BYM-model
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA users,

I have a question that might be a bit technical. Any help would be appreciated.

I have read the paper An intuitive Bayesian spatial model for disease mapping that accounts for scaling.

I do not quite follow on the sparse-ness property of the BYM-model, which is derived in the paper. In the paper it is stated that the precision matrix of [w1,w2] is

Q_tot=
[ tau/(1-phi) I-matrix,-sqrt{phi*tau}/(1-phi) I-matrix   ]
[ -sqrt{phi*tau}/(1-phi) I-matrix, Q_*+phi/(1-phi) I-matrix    ]

where I is an identity-matrix.

If we invert  Q_tot and then consider the lower right block of this matrix, i.e. the covariance matrix for the spatial term, (call it Sigma22) and then invert this, we get Sigma_22^{-1}=Q_*, which is sparse. But have we not enforced a sum to zero constraint on w_2? Then the precision matrix should not be sparse? We should have that Sigma_22 = Q^(-1)-Q^(-1)t(A)((AQ^(-1)t(A)))^(-1)AQ^(-1)   (Taken from Rues book).

I have tried to illustrate the calculations using the Germany-dataset and the example used in the help-section for the function  inla.scale.model <https://rdrr.io/github/INBO-BMK/INLA/man/scale.model.html>.

Where am I wrong?

#Example start

#Small number to be added to the diagonal of Q

eps = sqrt(.Machine$double.eps)

library(INLA)

data(Germany)

g = system.file("demodata/germany.graph", package="INLA")

source(system.file("demodata/Bym-map.R", package="INLA"))

Q = -inla.graph2matrix(g)

diag(Q) = 0

diag(Q) = -rowSums(Q)

n = dim(Q)[1]

Q.scaled = inla.scale.model(Q, constr = list(A = matrix(1, 1, n), e=0))

Q.scaled

Q.scaled.eps=Q.scaled+diag(n)*eps

A=matrix(1, 1, n)

tau_b=0.5

phi=0.5

I=Matrix(0,n,n,sparse=TRUE)

diag(I)=1

upper=cbind(tau_b/(1-phi)*I,-sqrt(phi*tau_b)/(1-phi)*I)

lower=cbind(-sqrt(phi*tau_b)/(1-phi)*I,Q.scaled.eps+phi/(1-phi)*I)

Precision=rbind(upper,lower)

Sigma=solve(Precision)

#Extract the covariance matrix for the spatial term

Sigma.spatial=Sigma[(n+1):(2*n),(n+1):(2*n)]

diag(Q.scaled.eps)-diag(solve(Sigma.spatial))

#The diagonals match

solve(Sigma.spatial)

#Which is sparse,

 #We see that the elements are the same.  One example:

Q.scaled.eps[544,534]

solve(Sigma.spatial)[544,534]

#However, is w2~sim N(0,Q.scaled.eps^-1) or N(0,Q.scaled^-) where Q.scaled^- is #the generalized variance.

#What is the sigma of the spatial term under sum to zero constraint? Expression from Rue's book.

A=matrix(1, 1, n)

Component1=as.matrix(solve(Q.scaled.eps))

Component2=as.matrix(solve(Q.scaled.eps)%*%t(A)%*%solve(A%*%solve(Q.scaled.eps)%*%t(A))%*%A%*%solve(Q.scaled.eps))

Sigma.spatial.correct=Component1-Component2

diag(Sigma.spatial.correct)-diag(solve(Q.scaled.eps))

#These do not match, as expected.

#Example end
Best regards

Fredrik

To: R-inla discussion group <r-inla-disc...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: [r-inla] The sparse parametrisation of the BYM-model

Dear INLA users,

I have a question that might be a bit technical. Any help would be appreciated.

I have read the paper An intuitive Bayesian spatial model for disease mapping that accounts for scaling.

I do not quite follow on the sparse-ness property of the BYM-model, which is derived in the paper. In the paper it is stated that the precision matrix of [w1,w2] is

Q_tot=
[ tau/(1-phi) I-matrix,-sqrt{phi*tau}/(1-phi) I-matrix   ]
[ -sqrt{phi*tau}/(1-phi) I-matrix, Q_*+phi/(1-phi) I-matrix    ]

where I is an identity-matrix.

If we invert  Q_tot and then consider the lower right block of this matrix, i.e. the covariance matrix for the spatial term, (call it Sigma22) and then invert this, we get Sigma_22^{-1}=Q_*, which is sparse. But have we not enforced a sum to zero constraint on w_2? Then the precision matrix should not be sparse? We should have that Sigma_22 = Q^(-1)-Q^(-1)t(A)((AQ^(-1)t(A)))^(-1)AQ^(-1)   (Taken from Rues book).

I have tried to illustrate the calculations using the Germany-dataset and the example used in the help-section for the function  inla.scale.model <https://rdrr.io/github/INBO-BMK/INLA/man/scale.model.html>.

Where am I wrong?

#Example start

#Small number to be added to the diagonal of Q

eps = sqrt(.Machine$double.eps)

library(INLA)

data(Germany)

g = system.file("demodata/germany.graph", package="INLA")

source(system.file("demodata/Bym-map.R", package="INLA"))

Q = -inla.graph2matrix(g)

diag(Q) = 0

diag(Q) = -rowSums(Q)

n = dim(Q)[1]

Q.scaled = inla.scale.model(Q, constr = list(A = matrix(1, 1, n), e=0))

Q.scaled

Q.scaled.eps=Q.scaled+diag(n)*eps

A=matrix(1, 1, n)

tau_b=0.5

phi=0.5

I=Matrix(0,n,n,sparse=TRUE)

diag(I)=1

upper=cbind(tau_b/(1-phi)*I,-sqrt(phi*tau_b)/(1-phi)*I)

lower=cbind(-sqrt(phi*tau_b)/(1-phi)*I,Q.scaled.eps+phi/(1-phi)*I)

Precision=rbind(upper,lower)

Sigma=solve(Precision)

#Extract the covariance matrix for the spatial term

Sigma.spatial=Sigma[(n+1):(2*n),(n+1):(2*n)]

diag(Q.scaled.eps)-diag(solve(Sigma.spatial))

#The diagonals match

solve(Sigma.spatial)

#Which is sparse,

 #We see that the elements are the same.  One example:

Q.scaled.eps[544,534]

solve(Sigma.spatial)[544,534]

#However, is w2~sim N(0,Q.scaled.eps^-1) or N(0,Q.scaled^-) where Q.scaled^- is #the generalized variance.

#What is the sigma of the spatial term under sum to zero constraint? Expression from Rue's book.

A=matrix(1, 1, n)

Component1=as.matrix(solve(Q.scaled.eps))

Component2=as.matrix(solve(Q.scaled.eps)%*%t(A)%*%solve(A%*%solve(Q.scaled.eps)%*%t(A))%*%A%*%solve(Q.scaled.eps))

Sigma.spatial.correct=Component1-Component2

diag(Sigma.spatial.correct)-diag(solve(Q.scaled.eps))

#These do not match, as expected.

#Example end
Best regards

Fredrik

messages.body_plain:
Yes, I believe that is correct. INLA uses 'conditioning by Kriging' to correct for the constraints while retaining the sparsity of the Q matrix. See section 2.3.3 of Rue and Held (and eqn 2.31 for how to efficiently calculate the conditional density, which I glossed over too quickly on my first **several** reads...).

Thanks,
Jeff

messages.subject: Installation difficulties
messages.subject_clean: Installation difficulties
messages.body_plain:
I experienced installation difficulties on Fedora 32.
Multiple failed installation attempts with repetitive downloads of more than 300MB of packaged data.

I suggest the package maintainer include a code that check prerequisites before downloading the entire package.

A straightforward installation attempt using the first lines of code on the download page returned a series of errors.
Instead I installed Bioconductor, the Bioconductor core packages and then used a single script to install prerequisites:
BiocManager::install(c("graph","Rgraphviz","sf","rgdal","rgl","spdep"))
A package (foreach) had to be updated at this point, which caused a second INLA installation failure.
I reinstalled the necessary package (foreach), then I ran the install script for the stable package from the download page, and succeeded.
install.packages("INLA", repos=c(getOption("repos"), INLA="https://inla.r-inla-download.org/R/stable"), dep=TRUE)

Hi,

thanks for pointing to the note, I had forgot about that one. That is my
notes for that model (and the computations of the pc-prior).

This way of writing it, on page 3, will preserve sparsity.

the sum-to-zero constraint, is imposed, as Jeff said, afterwards, by
doing a rank one correction (also to the density) as described in the
GMRF book.  (the ``conditioning by Kriging'' stuff, but using Bayes
formula for the density)

Best
H

messages.body_plain:
Hi INLAgroup,

I use the following to scale the model for spatio-temporal interaction type fourth:

H <- inla.read.graph(filename="LDN.graph")
graph <-(inla.graph2matrix(H))
graph <- -graph
diag(graph) <- H$nnbs

Cmatrix=kronecker(rw1,graph)

R=ginv(Cmatrix)
G2=exp(mean(log(diag(R))))
G3=Cmatrix*G2

but the log(diag(R)) produces  NaNs. So I decided to use inla.scale.model function like knmodels.R illustrated "https://github.com/inbo/INLA/blob/master/R/knmodels.R"
to scale the model.

R.t <- inla.scale.model(crossprod(diff(Diagonal(t))),
                                    constr=list(A=matrix(1,1,t), e=0))

R.s <- inla.scale.model(Diagonal(n, colSums(graph)) - graph,
                         constr=list(A=matrix(1, 1, n), e=0))
Cmatrix=kronecker(R.t,R.s)

Am I correct?

Thanks in advance for your help and time.

Bests,
Leila

Hi

I think this relates to how 'ginv' defines zero.

INLA:::inla.ginv()

is a modification to 'ginv' which allow you to define 'rankdef=...'
which is the known rank-deficiancy (if you know that). then you'll get
it right, rw1 have rankdef=1, and so with graph (if its connectected),
and then you know the rankdef of the kronecker product.

H

> > > > model, which is derived in the paper. In the paper it is stated
> > > > that the precision matrix of [w1,w2] is
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Q_tot=
> > > > [ tau/(1-phi) I-matrix,-sqrt{phi*tau}/(1-phi) I-matrix   ]

> > > >
> > > > where I is an identity-matrix.
> > > >
> > > > If we invert  Q_tot and then consider the lower right block of
> > > > this matrix, i.e. the covariance matrix for the spatial term,
> > > > (call it Sigma22) and then invert this, we get Sigma_22^{-1}=Q_*,
> > > > which is sparse. But have we not enforced a sum to zero constraint
> > > > on w_2? Then the precision matrix should not be sparse? We should
> > > > have that Sigma_22 = Q^(-1)-Q^(-1)t(A)((AQ^(-1)t(A)))^(-1)AQ^(-1)

> > > >

> > > >
> > > > n = dim(Q)[1]
> > > >
> > > > Q.scaled = inla.scale.model(Q, constr = list(A = matrix(1, 1, n),
> > > > e=0))
> > > >
> > > > Q.scaled
> > > >
> > > > Q.scaled.eps=Q.scaled+diag(n)*eps
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > A=matrix(1, 1, n)

> > > >

> > > >

> > > >
> > > > diag(I)=1
> > > >
> > > > upper=cbind(tau_b/(1-phi)*I,-sqrt(phi*tau_b)/(1-phi)*I)
> > > >
> > > > lower=cbind(-sqrt(phi*tau_b)/(1-phi)*I,Q.scaled.eps+phi/(1-phi)*I)
> > > >
> > > > Precision=rbind(upper,lower)
> > > >
> > > > Sigma=solve(Precision)
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > #Extract the covariance matrix for the spatial term

> > > >
> > > >
> > > >

> > > >
> > > >

messages.subject: Re: How can I evaluate the model performance?
messages.subject_clean: How can I evaluate the model performance?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kuan,

Here is some code that shows common model and variable evaluation methods.

Best,
Tim

# data
n <- 50; a <- 40; b <- -1.5; sigma2 <- 50; x1 <- 1:n
x2 <- sample(1:n); g1 <- sample(gl(5, 10))
eps <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd=sqrt(sigma2))
y <- a + b*x1 + eps; hist(y)
plot(x1, y)
plot(x2, y)
plot(g1, y)

# run competing models
library(INLA)
library(brinla) # for evaluating random effects
dat <- data.frame(y, x1, x2, g1)
r0 <- inla(y ~ 1, data=dat, family="gaussian",
           control.compute=list(cpo=T, waic=T, dic=T, config=T))
r1 <- inla(y ~ 1 + x1, data=dat, family="gaussian",
           control.compute=list(cpo=T, waic=T, dic=T, config=T))
r2 <- inla(y ~ 1 + x1 + x2, data=dat, family="gaussian",
           control.compute=list(cpo=T, waic=T, dic=T, config=T))
r3 <- inla(y ~ 1 + x1 + x2 + f(g1, model="iid"), data=dat, family="gaussian",
           control.compute=list(cpo=T, waic=T, dic=T, config=T))

# compare models with information criteria (lowest is best)
r0$waic$waic; r1$waic$waic; r2$waic$waic; r3$waic$waic
r0$dic$dic; r1$dic$dic; r2$dic$dic; r3$dic$dic

# compare models with cross validation (lowest is best)
cval <- function(result=r1){
  test <- sum(result$cpo$failure)
  if(test != 0) print("some cpo estimates failed the quality test. do not use.")
  return(-2 * sum(log(result$cpo$cpo), na.rm = T))
}
cval(r0); cval(r1); cval(r2); cval(r3)

# pick a model and get credible intervals for fixed effects
r1$summary.fixed[,c(1,3,5)]

# get posterior probability that a parameter estimate is positive
1 - inla.pmarginal(0, r2$marginals.fixed$x2)

# get variation explained by random effects
brinla::bri.hyperpar.summary(r3)[, c(1,3,5)]

# look at model fit to data
hist(r1$cpo$pit) # should be uniformish
plot(r1$summary.fitted.values$mean, dat$y); abline(0,1)
# x values are posterior mean fitted values that include fixed and random effects

messages.subject: Problem formulating a marked point process model
messages.subject_clean: Problem formulating a marked point process model
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm trying to create a sort of marked point process model and am not quite getting the format right (I think - whenever I try running it I get endless messages

"Function: GMRFLib_build_sparse_matrix_TAUCS(), Line: 758, Thread: 0
Variable evaluates to NAN or INF. idx=(1577,1577). I will try to fix it..."
).

I suspect I'm getting something wrong in the structure, and it might be to do with the Intercept (I've played around a lot to see if I can isolate things), but I can't quite work out how this relates to the int.vp (an intercept for the points object only - does that makes sense?).

Essentially I have two data stacks, one of point data, one of background data, which I combine and then fit with a log link and appropriate (I think!) spde model.

Each point belongs to one of two groups (indicated by a 0 / 1 column called selous in the points data) and I have a few spatial covariates. A key question is whether there is a strong impact of the mark on the relationship with the covariates. I have tried to test this by specifying an interaction between the mark and the covariates in the formula, but this could be completely wrong!

My code is:

library(INLA)
load("testData.Rdata")

# stk.ip - defines the background data
# stk.points - defines the point data
# mesh - mesh for...
# spde - the spatial structure

# important note: selous only appears in the points data, because it is a property of the points (a mark)
# other data should be present for both points and background

form <- formula(resp ~ 0 + selous * (PA2 + PA3 + PA4 + rivers.s) + int.vp + Intercept +
                  f(i, model = spde))

# combine data stacks:
stck <- inla.stack(stk.ip, stk.points)

#priors:
cont.fix <- list(
  mean = list(int.vp = 0),
  mean.intercept = 0,
  prec = list(int.vp = 1),
  prec.intercept = 0.001
)

# Fit model
mod <- inla(form, family = "poisson", control.family = list(list(link = "log")),
            data = inla.stack.data(stck),
            verbose = TRUE,
            control.results = list(return.marginals.random = FALSE,
                                   return.marginals.predictor = FALSE),
            control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stck),  link = NULL, compute = TRUE),
            control.fixed = cont.fix,
            Ntrials = inla.stack.data(stck)$Ntrials,
            E = inla.stack.data(stck)$e,
            num.threads = 6)

And the testData.Rdata file can be found here: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Spf_uJFyKvf_EXyPh5h0P0wHp85wTdJs/view?usp=sharing

Any ideas could be most welcome! It's probably something fairly basic - I'm still not getting my head around all of this.

Thanks!

Colin

messages.body_plain:
Hello dear INLA community,

I'm working with a very large spatial dataset with 1,134,465 points. I believe I'm facing a memory issue, as I've only 16gb. I've followed lots of threads regarding the subject and I've tried different things to workaround. I used num.threads, diagonal, int.strategy='eb', verbose=TRUE, and none worked. Lately I've been working with a subset with 16,000 points (you can see that option in my code), though for the prediction it's essential that I have the same resolution as the original raster, so the prediction grid is huge and when I run inla(), it crashes.

I attached my code so maybe you can see a mistake that I don't. This code was shrunk for the post, as it had a comparison between different models with different covariates. It has only the model chosen for predictions (r.lin.srtmL).

Do you have any idea how to workaround this issue or is it only memory that will probably fix it? I still have the possibility to access a 32gb RAM PC, though with Windows, which crashes more often when using INLA.

Thank you on advance!

Huriel Reichel

messages.body_plain:
The e>0,resp=1, e=0,resp=1 thing is how the lgcp likelihood is implemented, so that's by INLA design...

But the scaling is a likely problem, yes. If your space is in metres (default UTM coordinates, for example), then rescaling to kilometres is highly recommended.
This would change the scale of E by a factor 1e6, so 1e8 would become a much more well-behaved 100.

Finn

I have used 'e' to determine weight based on the area of the observation - for points this is zero, but for background data it indicase essentially the mesh resolution. I could rescale to coordinates to make this much smaller when non-zero if this will help, or I could have just miss-understood how this would work!

> > > want to scale the problem/data so its more 'well behaved
> > >
> > > it seems like all 'resp' is 0 when e > 0 and 1 when e=0. I guess this is
> > > not what you want ?
> > >
> > > H
> > >
> > >

> > > >

> > > > ).
> > > >
> > > > I suspect I'm getting something wrong in the structure, and it might

> > > > isolate things), but I can't quite work out how this relates to the
> > > > int.vp (an intercept for the points object only - does that makes
> > > > sense?).
> > > >
> > > > Essentially I have two data stacks, one of point data, one of
> > > > background data, which I combine and then fit with a log link and
> > > > appropriate (I think!) spde model.
> > > >
> > > > Each point belongs to one of two groups (indicated by a 0 / 1 column
> > > > called selous in the points data) and I have a few spatial covariates.
> > > > A key question is whether there is a strong impact of the mark on the
> > > > relationship with the covariates. I have tried to test this by
> > > > specifying an interaction between the mark and the covariates in the
> > > > formula, but this could be completely wrong!
> > > >
> > > > My code is:
> > > >
> > > > library(INLA)
> > > > load("testData.Rdata")
> > > >
> > > > # stk.ip - defines the background data
> > > > # stk.points - defines the point data
> > > > # mesh - mesh for...
> > > > # spde - the spatial structure
> > > >
> > > > # important note: selous only appears in the points data, because it
> > > > is a property of the points (a mark)
> > > > # other data should be present for both points and background
> > > >
> > > > form <- formula(resp ~ 0 + selous * (PA2 + PA3 + PA4 + rivers.s) +
> > > > int.vp + Intercept +
> > > >                   f(i, model = spde))
> > > >
> > > > # combine data stacks:
> > > > stck <- inla.stack(stk.ip, stk.points)
> > > >
> > > > #priors:
> > > > cont.fix <- list(
> > > >   mean = list(int.vp = 0),
> > > >   mean.intercept = 0,
> > > >   prec = list(int.vp = 1),
> > > >   prec.intercept = 0.001
> > > > )
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > # Fit model
> > > > mod <- inla(form, family = "poisson", control.family = list(list(link
> > > > = "log")),
> > > >             data = inla.stack.data(stck),
> > > >             verbose = TRUE,
> > > >             control.results = list(return.marginals.random = FALSE,
> > > >                                    return.marginals.predictor =
> > > > FALSE),
> > > >             control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stck),  link =
> > > > NULL, compute = TRUE),
> > > >             control.fixed = cont.fix,
> > > >
> > > >             Ntrials = inla.stack.data(stck)$Ntrials,
> > > >             E = inla.stack.data(stck)$e,
> > > >             num.threads = 6)
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > And the testData.Rdata file can be found here:
> > > > https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Spf_uJFyKvf_EXyPh5h0P0wHp85wTdJs/view?usp=sharing
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Any ideas could be most welcome! It's probably something fairly basic
> > > > - I'm still not getting my head around all of this.
> > > >
> > > > Thanks!
> > > >
